report:
### Conclusion
The claim that capsaicin treats breast cancer in humans is currently **unsupported by clinical evidence**.

### Evidence Summary
While preliminary laboratory (*in vitro*) experiments demonstrate that capsaicin can inhibit proliferation and induce programmed cell death (apoptosis) in human breast cancer cell lines, these findings do not translate to an established medical treatment in living humans.

The main reasons supporting the view that this claim is false or unproven include:

* **Lack of Human Studies**: The vast majority of research into capsaicin's anti-cancer properties has been conducted on isolated cell cultures and animal models, with virtually no clinical proof of efficacy in living human cancer patients (https://www.canceractive.com/article/capsicum-cayenne-chilli-pepper-and-cancer).
* **Delivery and Bioavailability Barriers**: Translating cell-culture findings to human therapy presents major hurdles. In lab tests, cancer cells are exposed to capsaicin for up to 48 hours, whereas orally ingested capsaicin remains in the human bloodstream for under 90 minutes, making effective delivery to tumor sites highly uncertain (https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/spicy-peppers-breast-cancer/).
* **Speculative Clinical Utility**: Scientific reviews emphasize that the clinical value of oral capsaicin as a primary or complementary treatment alongside chemotherapy remains speculative rather than proven (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10177684/).

Consequently, capsaicin is not an approved or proven treatment for breast cancer in humans.
